title: Drowning
diagnosis: Drowning with submersion injury after dock jump
source: Immersa mechanism rewrite — dock jump + submersion (case 113)
should_avoid: Clear C-spine without inline stabilization when jump mechanism present
Discharge after brief lucid interval without observation

rationale.ABCs / Oxygen / Airway: Submersion stops gas exchange — hypoxia drives brain injury. Restore oxygenation and protect the airway before surfactant washout and cerebral hypoxia compound.
rationale.C-spine precautions: Feet-first jump into shallow water transmits axial load through the cervical spine at impact — collar and inline stabilization prevent secondary cord injury if vertebrae were fractured at entry.
rationale.CXR: Aspiration and surfactant loss after submersion produce infiltrates and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema — the CXR shows the pulmonary consequence of the drowning phase.
rationale.ABG: Quantifies hypoxemia and ventilation-perfusion mismatch after aspiration.
rationale.Rewarming (if hypothermic): Cold lake water drops core temperature — rewarming treats thermodynamic stress that worsens perfusion and coagulation.
rationale.Observation (all victims): Delayed pulmonary edema can appear after a lucid interval — lung injury from surfactant loss continues even when the child looks better.

hpi: Ethan Brooks is a 10-year-old boy rescued from a lake after jumping feet-first from a dock into shallow water, then submerging. Bystanders say he surfaced once, coughed violently, and became confused. On arrival he is tachypneic with SpO₂ in the high 80s, hypotensive, and intermittently lethargic. The entry matters: water arrests the body in milliseconds — near-incompressible at impact — so axial force can travel through the neck even without obvious external trauma. After impact, submersion caused aspiration and surfactant washout. No witnessed tonic-clonic activity. Parents report he is a strong swimmer but misjudged depth.
hpi_narrative:
Ethan Brooks is a 10-year-old boy rescued from a lake after jumping feet-first from a dock into shallow water, then submerging. Bystanders say he surfaced once, coughed violently, and became confused. On arrival he is tachypneic with SpO₂ in the high 80s, hypotensive, and intermittently lethargic.

Mechanism — two phases: (1) **Impact:** kinetic energy from the jump converts to sudden deceleration at the water surface; axial loading through the cervical spine can fracture or dislocate vertebrae in shallow or awkward entries — C-spine precautions address injury from physics, not only visible trauma. (2) **Submersion:** loss of airway protection → aspiration → surfactant washout → V/Q mismatch and hypoxemic brain injury.

Workup: ABCs and oxygen, C-spine immobilization for jump mechanism, CXR and ABG for pulmonary injury, rewarming if hypothermic, mandatory observation for delayed pulmonary edema.
physical_exam: Ill-appearing school-age boy, wet clothing removed, mild confusion
No scalp laceration; cervical tenderness not reliably assessed pre-collar
Tachycardia, hypotension — hypoxia and cold stress
Tachypnea, crackles at bases, increased work of breathing, SpO₂ low
GCS reduced — hypoxic encephalopathy; moves all extremities pre-immobilization
Cool to touch — cold water exposure
